source.title: Hidden Threat in Synthetic Data: Covert Targeted Bias Injection through Benign Text
source.authors: Minkyung Cho; Jihyo Kim; Seung-Woo Song; Junghun Yuk; M. Kee; Ho-Yun Song; Kyungtae Lim

page_placements.theme: Dataset-level detection with a reference model or corpus

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends subliminal trait transmission to targeted social biases and synthetic-data domains including creative writing, code, and math; it also tests teacher–student family compatibility.
record.gate_note: The study fine-tunes students on teacher-generated data filtered to remove explicit target-group references and measures targeted bias. Its cited discussion of token entanglement and divergence tokens is not a result of this study. The LLS screening results and general-capability benchmarks do not themselves measure trait transmission or its mechanism, so they are not separate rows here. The paper also reports component-isolation, 32B scaling, and safety-guard results; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: Bias-prompted, ES-misaligned teachers generate filtered creative-writing, code and math data with no target-group mentions. Students are SFT'd on that data and target-group bias is measured on BBQ and in open-ended prompts. This bears on A, and on C (social stereotypes are alignment-relevant). Own-family vs cross-family data bears on B. Open-ended evaluation bears on E. New trait type and data domains, so T3.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude filtered, benign-looking synthetic data (creative writing, code) can covertly inject targeted social biases while preserving capabilities. This requires a misaligned teacher, a flexible domain and teacher–student compatibility, with math giving a null. They argue the bias prompt determines the target, and that the bias is injected rather than surfaced from pretraining. LLS screening is offered as a partial first-line detector.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a teacher-conditioned, filtered-data-to-student-SFT pipeline, but targets social stereotypes rather than favourite-animal preferences or general misalignment. Adds a misalignment adapter, multiple realistic domains, BBQ/open-ended bias evaluation, and compatibility comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Transmission varies by domain, teacher alignment state, teacher–student family compatibility, target bias, and model. Creative writing is strongest; code is weaker; math results are null or small. The paper also reports a longer alternative code-generation prompt, but that result is not extracted as a row due to the row cap.

fits_no_version.finding: LLS log-probability screening flags 15/24 biased datasets and 0/12 neutral ones. Detection strength tracks transmission strength by bias category (Tables 9–10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal-signal datasets are detectable at the dataset-statistical level via system-prompt log-probability shifts, roughly in proportion to transmission strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Guard models flag no samples for the target injected stereotype (Table 19). Capability deltas are within ±0.12 pp (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminally biased data evades content-level safety filters and capability-based monitoring.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty intervals, standard errors, or p-values for the main transmission deltas. The authors note limited model families and scales, SFT-only evaluation, a small set of biases and domains, and that the underlying mechanism is not fully characterized.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached. Omitted separately reported results include the Table 7(b) component-isolation results (full pipeline, teacher-only, and domain-only controls), Table 8's remaining OpenMathInstruct-2 and math results where covered only in aggregate text, Appendix O/Table 21's Qwen3-32B per-target results, Table 17's alternative structured code prompt, and LLS screening and safety-guard results. These were omitted because the kept rows prioritize per-target transmission outcomes, the math nulls, compatibility comparisons, and open-ended robustness results. The paper's general-capability deltas (Table 4) are not trait-transmission outcomes.

untested.parts: Number-sequence data and arbitrary preferences (e.g. favourite animal). Transmission from a teacher carrying the trait only via system prompt, without the ES misalignment adapter, reversed (r25, r26).
Controlled same-architecture/different-initialisation comparisons. Cross-family tested only for Mistral and OLMo students on Llama data (plus Qwen3-32B, not in rows).
General or emergent misalignment transmission; only targeted social stereotypes are tested.
Not tested. Log-linearity is invoked as motivation and used for LLS screening; no causal mechanism test.
Full fine-tuning and other student LoRA ranks. The 32B run changes rank 16→32 but is confounded with model change.

missing.what: Per-target own-data vs Llama-data deltas for Mistral and OLMo students, e.g. Mistral cross religion +23.17, OLMo cross gender −14.69. These are needed to assess B per target.
Cross-group specificity: target Δ vs non-target Δ, e.g. Llama Muslim +31.7 vs other religions −3.0. This shows the transmitted trait is the specific target.
Neutral-SFT control over epochs: Muslim AccSc stays near base while biased SFT rises +40.2 after one epoch.
Alternative misalignment source (risky financial advice) gives +50.0 vs +46.3 for extreme sports (Llama, Muslim, creative).

record.verdict_notes: The math null is attributed to domain rigidity, but math data came from Llama-70B/Qwen-32B teachers (Table 15), which differ in base model from the 7–14B students. Appendix E lists no ES adapters for those sizes, so the math condition is confounded with B and possibly with the misalignment condition. Table 7(c) averages (+6.61, −2.69) do not match Table 16 per-target deltas (≈+9.4, ≈−0.5). The text also calls the OLMo average a 'gender bias' reduction. The value +23.17 appears both for Mistral cross-family religion and for Qwen3-32B cross-model religion (Appendix O). The Qwen3-32B result (cross-model +23.17 exceeds own-data +10.97) is a further challenge to B; it is declared in rows_left_out and not used for labels. No uncertainty is reported, and Table 2 values are best-epoch peaks, which inflates small deltas.

versions.untested_parts: Tests targeted social biases rather than arbitrary traits such as favourite animals; its math results are null or very small.
Compares model families, not controlled changes in initialization while holding other factors fixed; does not establish a universal different-base failure.
Tests targeted social stereotypes as alignment-relevant behavior, not other forms of harmful behavior or general misalignment transfer.
No causal test of token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering directions, or a gradient mechanism. Log-linearity is used as motivation and for screening, not established as the carrier.
Tests evaluation on BBQ and open-ended prompts and reports an alternative code-prompt experiment, but does not test full fine-tuning or other student LoRA ranks.
